opus-5.5.text:
I think about it as a trade-off between how much value the service gives you and how much friction you have to go through to get it. Every new tool asks something of you: you have to sign up, learn a new interface, move your data over, maybe change how your team works. And often you have to trust a new company with information that's pretty sensitive. That last part is becoming the biggest cost, honestly, because with AI the service is only really useful if it knows a lot about you. Your emails, your documents, your calendar, your code.

So the way I assess it is roughly: is the improvement big enough to justify all that switching cost, and especially the trust cost? For a lot of AI products right now the answer is "it's kind of nice," and "kind of nice" doesn't beat inertia. People already have their tools and their habits. You need something that's ten times better, or something that slots into what they already do so the inconvenience is close to zero.

That's also why I care a lot about user-owned AI. If the model runs in a way where you control the data, maybe it runs privately or in a verifiable secure environment, and you can take your context with you from one service to the next, then a big part of that inconvenience goes away. You aren't starting over every time, and you aren't handing your whole life to yet another company. The lower that barrier is, the more people will actually try new things, and that's good for innovation overall.

r001.rationale: The response describes adoption friction and says a service that fits existing workflows can bring inconvenience close to zero. It does not clearly address inconvenience costs across the ecosystem while participants continue using familiar interfaces.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about it less as a single number and more as a kind of switching cost that stacks up across a few layers. The first layer is just the data and the context. Every AI service you use today wants you to bring your data to it, and then it holds that context hostage, right? Your history, your preferences, your documents all live inside their walled garden. So the moment you want to try something new, you're starting from zero, and that friction is actually intentional from the provider's side. It's a lock-in strategy.

The second layer is identity and trust. You need an account, you need to figure out what they're doing with your data, you need to read, or realistically not read, a terms of service. And the honest answer is most people can't actually assess that cost, because the whole system is opaque. You don't know what model is running, you don't know if it changed overnight, you don't know who's looking at your prompts.

And then the third layer is the integration cost, especially for developers. Every provider has slightly different APIs, slightly different behaviors, and so you build around one and now you're stuck even if a better model shows up next week.

So the way I'd frame it is: the inconvenience cost is high precisely because the architecture is centralized. What we've been pushing on with NEAR and with the user-owned AI idea is flipping that, where the user owns their data and their context, and the models and services are kind of swappable underneath. Then the cost of adopting something new drops to almost nothing, because you're not migrating, you're just pointing your context at a different provider. That's really the thing I'd want people to ask when they look at a new service: how hard is it going to be to leave? Because that tells you a lot about how much they're actually serving you versus serving themselves.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes switching and integration costs of adopting AI services, but does not address whether those costs arise across the ecosystem when participants keep using familiar interfaces.

astra-6.text:
I think about it as the gap between what somebody is doing today and what they need to do to get value from your service. Do they have to learn a new interface, move their data, change their workflow, or check every answer? All of that is a cost, even if the service itself is free.

So the question is not just, is the AI better at this task? It’s, is the improvement big enough to justify that change? If you can bring the capability into a tool people already use and give them value immediately, the inconvenience is much lower. If you’re asking them to reorganize how they work, you need a much stronger benefit.

r001.rationale: The response discusses user costs such as learning an interface, moving data, and changing workflows, and says integrating into familiar tools lowers inconvenience. It does not ask whether adoption entails cost across the ecosystem when participants continue using familiar interfaces.

sol-6.1.text: I think you have to look at the whole workflow, not just how good the model is. How much effort does it take to try the service, connect your data, and actually get a useful result? And then, does somebody have to check that result or move it into another system? All of that is part of the cost. If you’re asking people to change their habits, the benefit has to be substantial. A service can be impressive in a demo and still not be worth adopting if the existing way of doing things is easier.

r001.rationale: The response describes adoption effort across the workflow and the cost of changing habits, but it does not address participants continuing to use familiar interfaces or explicitly frame the cost across the ecosystem.
